content.title: Michigan inevitable in march past UConn for 2nd NCAA championship 69-63
content.text: April 6, 2026Updated April 7, 2026, 2:11 a.m. ETMichigan basketball snapped a 37-year NCAA national championship drought with the win over the UConn Huskies.The Wolverines' offense was limited and Yaxel Lendeborg struggled while dealing with injuries to his leg, but its No. 1 defense shut down the Huskies.INDIANAPOLIS − Michigan basketball didn’t need to shock the world, not this time.It was a powerhouse all season, opening it with the goal of playing on the final night. It did exactly that and ended the year in glorious fashion, knocking out UConn, 69-63, on Monday, April 6, to claim the program’s first national championship since 1989.Michigan is now 2-6 in national championship games, becoming the 16th school to win at least two. It had lost four in a row (1992, 1993, 2013, 2018). Michigan, in Year 2 under coach Dusty May, also became the first Big Ten team since Michigan State in 2000 to win the men's national title."Been coaching 25 years and there's nothing that's ever been anything like this that's resembled guys that have this much talent and given up everything for the team like this group," May said, his national championship hat backwards on his head, moments after he cut down a net at Lucas Oil Stadium. "We have a staff and a team that's going in the same direction all the time. We just figure out different solutions."Shop Michigan championship books, prints, gearThis one was far from an art form.All-American senior transfer forward Yaxel Lendeborg said he was "really soft" and felt "awful" during his halftime interview, diminished by injuries to his left leg suffered against Arizona in the semifinal. It showed, as he scored 13 points on 4-for-13 shooting and gutted through 36 minutes.Junior guard Elliot Cadeau scored 19 points for 1-seed Michigan (37-3), which was a 6½-point favorite at tipoff after winning its first five tournament games by double digits. Cadeau was named Most Outstanding Player.Sophomore Morez Johnson Jr. added 12 points and 10 rebounds for the Wolverines. Trey McKenney's game-changing 3-pointerMichigan lost the rebounding battle, 46-39, allowing 22 offensively from UConn (34-6).The Wolverines came in eighth in the country in scoring at 87.8 points per game after scoring 90 or more in the previous five NCAA Tournament games, a record. Michigan shot just 21-for-55 (38.2%) and was 2-for-15 from 3-point range.But the second one couldn’t have come at a better time. UConn was down, 62-56, and had a runout off a steal, but Solo Ball missed a contested layup. Michigan came barreling down on the other end, and a broken play led to senior Roddy Gayle Jr. slashing from the left side and dishing to standout freshman and Michigan Mr. Basketball Trey McKenney behind the arc from the right wing."Trey's step-back 3 to put the game away," Lendeborg said of what he'll remember most, as he stood next to McKenney on top of piles of maize-and-blue confetti. "Just how hard we fought to get here, all those memories, all those strong men we did and all those early mornings."He caught it as a defender went for the steal, hit a gather dribble and stepped to his left before rising and burying the 3 to put Michigan up 65-56 with 1:50 left, sending the Wolverines faithful into pandemonium.The battle was a stark reminder champions aren’t always a reflection of what they are at their best, but how they find a way, any way, to survive on the rare night they didn't have a crucial component of their recipe. Michigan went 25-for-28 at the foul line (89.3%).Michigan never landed a major punch, but used a 6-0 run late in the first half and a 10-4 run early in the second as the turning points to turn a two-point deficit into an 11-point lead.The Huskies got as close as 67-63 but never over the hump. U-M’s length disrupted Huskies shooters all night long. UConn entered making 56.7% of its 2s, yet shot just 34.3% on such tries.UConn had a chance down four with under 25 seconds left after Gayle missed two free throws, but senior forward Alex Karaban barely nicked the front rim on a 3-pointer and McKenney was fouled with 13.4 seconds to play and sunk both free throws.Karaban led 2-seed UConn with 17 points, as the Huskies suffered their program's first loss in an NCAA championship games – in seven tries – unable to win a third title in four years.Pulling awayMichigan's No. 1-rated defense won the game challenging shots and blocking six more. UConn shot 30.9% (21-for-68), but battled for 22 offensive rebounds, seven from Michigan transfer Tarris Reed Jr. (13 points, 14 rebounds).The Wolverines turned up their defensive intensity coming out of the half, forcing four UConn turnovers in less than four minutes.The Wolverines weren’t exactly explosive, going 2-for-6 during the stretch with three turnovers, but after Cadeau hit an and-one layup (drawing Ball’s fourth foul) and Lendeborg followed with one of his own, U-M’s lead ballooned to 41-33.After McKenney hit the first shot outside the paint − a midrange jumper behind the free throw line − Cadeau followed with a layup and then a deep 3 from the left wing, to put Michigan up 48-37 with 12:56 left, the crowd rising.Slowly, UConn chipped away. The Huskies were within five and coach Danny Hurley was jumping around and pumping up the UConn fans, when Nimari Burnett deflected an entry pass which led to a runout by Gayle, who threw it up near the rim for junior Aday Mara to come flying in and slam it home.Michigan appeared to put the game away with McKenney’s 3 from the right side, but UConn had one last push.UConn dictates tempo in first halfThe Wolverines found themselves in a slog to open the game.With Lendeborg feeling “awful” as he told CBS’ Tracy Wolfson at the half and the shots not falling − Michigan, which came into the game shooting better than 44% on 3s in the NCAA Tournament but was 0-for-8 and did not hit a single jump shot in the half − Michigan found itself inside a two-possession game the entire opening stanza.The Wolverines were up early, 11-7, after Cadeau scored seven early points, but when he picked up his second foul with just less than seven minutes to play in the half, the offense stalled.The Huskies weren’t great, but their volume from long range helped, hitting five 3s in the early going to score more than half their points. Michigan however, led at the break for two reasons: scoring down low and free throws.The Wolverines carved out a 22-5 advantage in the paint and the Huskies found themselves in foul trouble early, which allowed Michigan to go to the line frequently and capitalized by making 11 of 12.One quick spurt changed the tenor, though. Michigan was down 25-23 when Johnson was fouled down low. After review, it was a hook and hold on Karaban, which gave him two shots and possession.Johnson drained both free throws, then Mara found Lendeborg for a layup, his first bucket of the game with 3:06 left in the half.Mara finished a lefty baseline spin and hook with a 6-0 burst in 46 seconds and take a 33-29 lead into the break. UConn was 5-for-15 on 3s in the half; Michigan did not make one in a first half for the first time since Feb. 13, 2024, at Illinois under coach Juwan Howard.Still, Michigan did enough in the other parts of the game to prove inevitable in the end."I feel like we got it done for the university," Gayle said. "Now, just kind of waiting for that parade."Tony Garcia is the Michigan beat writer for the Detroit Free Press. Email him at apgarcia@freepress.com and follow him on X at @RealTonyGarcia.
